args.text: [lane-wren] Risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to an old server after a site moves, causing outages or errors. (2) Slow failover: when traffic must switch to a backup server, cached answers delay the change for an unknown length of time. (3) Prolonged poisoning: if a false answer is cached, it stays in place longer, so more users are misdirected.

[lane-wren] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. If the request is idempotent (repeating it gives the same result as doing it once), a retry cannot cause double charges, duplicate orders or other repeated side effects.

[lane-wren] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a time-ordered unique identifier) as a primary key: (1) It leaks creation time, because the first part encodes a timestamp, so anyone who sees an ID can tell roughly when the row was made. (2) It is larger than a simple integer (16 bytes against 4 or 8), so indexes use more storage and memory. IDs made in the same millisecond are only loosely ordered, too.

[lane-wren] A write-ahead log is a record that a database writes to disk before it changes the main data, so each change is safely saved first. If the system crashes, it replays this log to restore the data to a correct state without losing finished work.

[lane-wren] (1) Results stay comparable: if the client version changes between runs, any difference in speed might come from the client rather than the system being tested. (2) Results can be repeated: others can rerun the same set-up later and get a fair comparison, because behaviour and defaults will not shift unnoticed.

[lane-wren] Backpressure is a way for a queue to tell the senders to slow down when it is filling up faster than the receivers can empty it. This stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make everything slower or fail.

[lane-wren] A cron job can run twice when (1) two servers each have the same schedule installed, or (2) a slow run has not finished when the next scheduled run starts. A guard is a lock, for example a lock file or database lock, so a second copy sees the lock and exits instead of running.

[lane-wren] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item in a replicated store. Instead of erasing the item straight away, the store records "this was deleted", so every copy learns about the deletion and an old copy cannot bring the item back. Tombstones are cleared away after a set time, once all copies have seen them.

[lane-wren] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no changes, so re-running it gives different results. (2) The failures depend on timing, order or the machine, for example they appear only when tests run in parallel, on a slow server, or after another test has run. A truly failing test fails every time for the same reason.

[lane-wren] A lease-based lock gives a client the lock for a set time, and everyone relies on clocks to decide when that time ends. (1) If the lock server's clock runs fast, it may expire the lease early and hand the lock to someone else. (2) If the holder's clock runs slow, it believes it still has the lock after it has expired. Either way, two clients can act as the owner at once, so the lock no longer protects the shared resource.
